comparison: Both evaluations support the finding that Δ9-THC increases ESC proliferation but not EpiLC proliferation (C3, C30-C35). OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of statistical methods and replicates, while peer reviewers emphasize the remarkably low effective dose (~1 nM) and describe the evidence as 'convincing.' Both agree the finding is well-supported.

Perfect agreement on CB1 receptor mechanism (C5, C42-C44). Both evaluations support the pharmacological inhibition data with SR141716 and Western blot analysis. OpenEval highlights the strong statistical significance (p=1.66×10⁻⁵), while peer reviewers emphasize this mechanistic finding strengthens the study's conclusions.

Both support metabolic reprogramming in ESCs (C7, C45, C49, C51, C54). OpenEval evaluates multiple complementary assays (WST-1, Mitotracker, Seahorse) with statistical rigor. Peer reviewers group these metabolic findings with glycolysis inhibition data (C63-C64) and metabolomics (C8, C57, C59-C60, C62), accepting the broad metabolic upregulation as consistent with increased proliferation.

OpenEval specifically evaluates glycolysis inhibition experiments (C63-C64) as critical mechanistic evidence with strong statistical significance. Peer reviewers incorporate this finding into their broader metabolic assessment (R3), stating that 2-deoxyglucose blocks proliferation and that effects depend on both CB1 signaling and glycolysis.

OpenEval evaluates metabolomics data (C8, C57-C60, C62) as supported by comprehensive mass spectrometry analysis. Peer reviewers include these metabolomic findings in their broader metabolic assessment, accepting the 'broad upregulation of metabolites' and 'upregulation of anabolic genes' as consistent with increased proliferation.

Both support the finding of modest transcriptional changes (C6, C65-C68). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis with PCA showing transcriptional changes are modest compared to metabolic changes. Peer reviewers explicitly note 'transcriptomic changes are modest overall' and accept this as a key finding.

Both support GO enrichment analysis findings (C69-C71). OpenEval evaluates the differential GO term enrichment between ESCs and EpiLCs as providing mechanistic insight. Peer reviewers accept the 'upregulation of anabolic genes, consistent with the increased proliferation rate in mESCs.'

Perfect agreement on PGCLC findings (C79-C83). Both evaluations support the increased double-positive PGCLC population and proliferation tracing data. OpenEval emphasizes the flow cytometry methodology and statistical significance, while peer reviewers affirm the moderate increase and accept the finding without critique.

Perfect agreement on Δ9-THC clearance data (C84-C86). Both evaluations support the mass spectrometry evidence ruling out persistent drug as an alternative explanation. OpenEval notes the appropriate detection limit, while peer reviewers highlight this as a key addition to the revised manuscript that addresses a critical alternative explanation.

Both support metabolic memory in PGCLCs (C9, C87-C89). OpenEval evaluates the direct metabolic measurements with modest but significant increases (p<0.05). Peer reviewers affirm this as a central finding, stating 'mouse primordial germ cell-like cells can have a memory of previous metabolic perturbations.'

Both support PGCLC transcriptomic findings (C10, C90-C93). OpenEval evaluates RNA-seq analysis with PCA and GO enrichment showing oxidative phosphorylation upregulation. Peer reviewers accept altered gene expression and metabolism consistent with increased proliferation, though they don't extensively discuss the quality degradation interpretation.

Both support downregulation of structural/adhesion genes in PGCLCs (C94-C97). OpenEval finds the 'degradation of quality' interpretation reasonable but notes functional assays would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers present the data without challenge but don't extensively discuss the quality interpretation.

Both support differential response between ESCs and EpiLCs (C4, C36-C38). OpenEval evaluates consistent evidence of no proliferative effect in EpiLCs at lower doses with cytotoxicity at 10 µM. Peer reviewers accept this as important cell-type specificity, stating 'Δ9-THC increases the proliferation rate of mESCs but not mEpiLCs.'

Both support selective metabolic effects in EpiLCs (C46-C47, C50-C53, C56). OpenEval notes effects on glycolysis but not mitochondrial respiration, consistent with primed cell metabolic phenotype. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their assessment of cell-type-specific responses.

Divergent evaluation certainty. OpenEval supports hESC findings (C39-C41) as statistically significant (p=0.004) and consistent with the hypothesis. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the data but cautioning 'it would be premature to conclude that the same effects will be observed in human cells' and noting these are 'preliminary results.'

OpenEval supports the modest decrease in hESC mitochondrial mass (C48, p=0.04) as consistent with differential response in primed-like cells. Peer reviewers include this in their UNCERTAIN assessment of hESC data, expressing caution about generalizability to human cells.

Both acknowledge limitations of hESC data (C120-C121). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting preliminary data are supported but authors appropriately recognize need for additional work. Peer reviewers similarly express caution about premature conclusions regarding human cells.

Divergent evaluation certainty. OpenEval rates epigenetic modifier findings (C72-C78) as UNCERTAIN, noting low fold-changes and lack of direct epigenetic mark measurements, calling the suggestion 'speculative without functional validation.' Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these as part of the transcriptomic analysis without explicit challenge, though they don't discuss functional significance.

Perfect agreement on oxidative stress data (C61). Both evaluations support this negative control finding. OpenEval notes the measurement is direct and appropriate for assessing oxidative stress. Peer reviewers don't challenge the finding and accept it as supporting data for metabolic characterization.

Both support background/context claims (C1, C11-C20). OpenEval notes these are appropriately cited literature establishing study rationale. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these contextual claims through acknowledgment of the study's public health significance, without challenging the background.

Both support background claims about the model system (C2, C21-C29). OpenEval notes these provide scientific context supported by established literature. Peer reviewers accept the ESC-EpiLC-PGCLC differentiation model as 'a well-characterized in vitro model' without challenge.

Both support discussion/interpretation claims contextualizing findings (C99-C102, C106, C108-C109, C112-C113, C115-C119). OpenEval notes these are appropriately supported by citations. Peer reviewers affirm novelty and significance, stating the study is 'valuable' and 'significant for public health.'

Both support authors' conclusions (C107, C110-C111, C114, C122). OpenEval notes these are well-supported by experimental evidence though some aspects remain speculative. Peer reviewers affirm the significance for public health and society's need to understand potential effects of Δ9-THC exposure.

OpenEval specifically evaluates the integration of metabolic memory evidence (C98) as the central conclusion well-supported by multi-omics approach. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their broader assessment of PGCLC findings, accepting that metabolic and transcriptional changes persist.

OpenEval supports the mechanistic synthesis comparing Δ9-THC effects to developmental metabolic transitions (C103-C105). Peer reviewers incorporate the cell-type specificity concept (C105) into their assessment of differential responses between ESCs and EpiLCs.

OpenEval supports the distinction between mitochondrial respiration components (C55), noting selective increase in maximal capacity without changes in basal or ATP-linked respiration supports the anabolic hypothesis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific mechanistic detail.
